_about: Document retrieval gold-standard for 'Underground' by Suelette Dreyfus (Project Gutenberg, 1997). 11 chapters + front/back matter. book.title: Underground: Hacking, Madness and Obsession on the Electronic Frontier

queries.question: What was the WANK worm and why was it politically significant?
gold_paragraphs: The WANK worm—Worms Against Nuclear Killers—was the first major computer worm bearing a political message, released into NASA's SPAN/DEC/HEPNET network in October 1989.
It was also the trigger for the creation of FIRST, the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams.
With WANK, life imitated art, since the term computer 'worm' came from John Brunner's sci-fi novel, The Shockwave Rider, about a politically motivated worm.

queries.question: Who created the WANK worm and what evidence pointed to Australian origin?
gold_paragraphs: The WANK worm is also believed to be the first worm written by an Australian, or Australians.
Even as investigators sniffed around electronic trails leading to France, it appears the perpetrator was hiding behind his computer and modem in Australia.
Likely as not, only an Australian would see the worm's link to the lyrics of Midnight Oil.

queries.question: What was SPAN and how did it relate to the WANK worm outbreak?
gold_paragraphs: SPAN—Space Physics Analysis Network—was a global DECNET-based network, primarily controlled by NASA.
The WANK worm spread through SPAN and its interconnected networks including HEPNET and DECNET.
NASA's SPAN security team would miss the mark...these officials should to this day be pronouncing the 'Oilz' version of the WANK worm as 'oil zee'.

queries.question: How did Australian hackers steal over $500,000 from Citibank in 1989?
gold_paragraphs: An elite group of Australian hackers has lifted more than $US500,000 ($580,000) out of America's Citibank in one of the daring hacking crimes in Australia's history.

The Australian connection is reported to have used a telephone in the foyer of Telecom's headquarters at 199 William Street in Melbourne to send a 2600-hertz signal giving them access to a trunk line and ultimately to a managerial access code for Citibank.
These are the elite 'freekers' of white collar crime.

Par had appeared deeply troubled over the matter for weeks. He didn't seem to mind telling the Feds how he had broken into various computers, but that's not what they were really looking for. They wanted him to rat.

queries.question: What distinctive style made Phoenix traceable across multiple hackings?
gold_paragraphs: Whenever he was creating a root shell—root access—for himself, he would always save it in the same filename and in the same location on the computer. In some instances, he even created accounts called 'Phoenix' for himself.
It was this consistency of style which had made things so much easier for admins to trace his movements.

queries.question: What were Pad and Gandalf accused of planning and what worm codes did they possess?
gold_paragraphs: In one of his hacking forays, Pad had discovered a file, apparently written by Eugene Spafford, which said he was concerned that some British hackers—read Pad and Gandalf—would create a new worm, based on the RTM worm, and release it into the Internet.
Gandalf and Pad had captured copies of various worm source codes. They fished around inside SPAN until they surfaced with a copy of the WANK worm.
Despite their growing library of worm code, Pad had no intention of writing a new worm based on these existing codes.

queries.question: How did the computer underground evolve from its early days to the time of the book's writing?
gold_paragraphs: In the beginning, the computer underground was a place, like the corner pub, open and friendly. Now, it has become an ephemeral expanse, where hackers occasionally bump into one another but where the original sense of open community has been lost.

The computer underground has changed over time, largely in response to the introduction of new computer crime laws across the globe and to numerous police crackdowns. This work attempts to document not only an important piece of Australian history, but also to show fundamental shifts in the underground—to show, in essence, how the underground has moved further underground.
